utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I do not think the microphones are working. Case number IT-95-13a-T, Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Williamson and Waespi and Sutherland for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Fila together with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic, I am the Defence attorney for Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask Mr. Dokmanovic whether he can hear me. Can you hear me? Thank you. Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the trial starts -- sorry, I just have one copy -- I would like to give you this famed memorandum that we spent so much time on with Mr. Wheeler, in the English language, so you can take it and put it in the library, but we have this one single copy in the English language.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The French court reporter does not hear. Someone will come and check. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We may proceed, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have checked in your library and you do not have a copy of this memorandum. I brought it so that you could have it. I do not know how to hand it over to you, from pages 95 to 140. That is the text of the memorandum so I can only give it to you as a present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On behalf of the court, we will gratefully accept it and make sure that it is put into the library and thank Mr. Fila very much for his kind donation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Before we move on to our next witness, I wonder whether I could ask the Prosecutor about the admissions because we were handed a document on 2nd March, "Draft Admissions by the Prosecutor" and Mr. Fila responded on 5th March with a response on the draft admissions. I wonder whether Mr. Niemann could tell us to what extent the Prosecution is ready to accept the submissions made by Mr. Fila in paragraph 10(1) through 10(5) of his document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the admissions made by the Defence from 10(1) to 10(5) are acceptable to the Prosecution and we have a document which has being given to the Defence which incorporates those matters and it is just a matter of that document being signed by Mr. Fila and by the defendant and that will complete the matter. My only concern is that we want to ensure that the Defence are fully aware of the effect of these admissions, that they -- I am not sure whether there is such a procedure under the law of Yugoslavia and it may be a procedure which is peculiar to the common law. The experiences that we have had in the Erdemovic case have certainly made the Prosecution very cautious of just proceeding into areas such as this, making an assumption that they are fully appreciated on the other side. I am not trying to be in any way rude to Mr. Fila and if I am, I apologise for that, but I am most concerned to ensure that both Mr. Fila and the accused are fully comfortable with these admissions so that we do not get into the situation which occurred in the Erdemovic case. I just say that; Mr. Fila has them. They are available for him to be signed and for his client to sign them and when he is ready hopefully they can be filed and they will take effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? Would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my response, I said what points I could accept, so I did not accept everything that you mentioned. 3, 7, 8, 10, 11 and 14. I know what I am accepting. And all of this is within that which I admitted in the minutes. It is related to Ovcara, namely, that 200 people were killed, that an exhumation was carried out and I have no objections to that with the exception of the ethnic composition which I mentioned, because, under point 4, I said that there were 5 Serbs; there is 2 and I asked for the OTP to prove that they were not Serbs as they had been claiming, out of those 200, I mean, so what I said, these seven points, I am going to sign that and I know exactly what I am signing. And I also told the defendant about this, but not the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Fila, there was probably a slight misunderstanding. I was referring to point 10(1) to (5) of your own document where you make submissions to be accepted or not to be accepted by the Prosecution, and actually I think also Mr. Niemann was addressing this particular point. My question to Mr. Niemann was whether the Prosecution was prepared to admit your submissions as set out in those points or paragraphs of your confidential Defence response to the Prosecutor's draft admissions. Anyway, I think it is very clear now. I understand that you will consider carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Then it is not quite clear. Then we have not understood each other correctly, because I understand Mr. Niemann differently, that he was talking about the document that he handed to me so that I would sign it, but from 10(1) to (5), that is quite clear. Those are my own proposals and of course if he accepts that, then I am going to give up on 51 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honours. I have misspoken. I did not realise. I thought your Honour was talking about the admissions from the Defence, not the other way around. We are not in a position to comment on those at the moment. They are under consideration. That is part of the Defence case. I am sorry, your Honour. I did mis-speak. I did not mean to comment on those. The admissions from the Defence side, now that we are in the Prosecution case, those matters are in hand, but insofar as the Defence case is concerned, we will advise Mr. Fila of our position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right, it is clear that so far we have no agreement on the admissions and so therefore we will proceed and maybe in one or two days the Prosecution and Defence could come back and file a document, hopefully signed by the Defence counsel and the accused. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I said in my response what I do accept and, since I said that I accepted it, I see no reason why I would not sign it, so let us not waste any time over that. If I understand you correctly, your Honour, the whole point of this exercise was to speed up matters, so I accepted everything that was supposed to be presented and there is no dispute between us on that point. So 3, 7, 8, 11, 12 and 14 of the Prosecution's proposal, we agree on that, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. It is very clear now. Thank you. I wonder whether the Prosecutor is prepared to call his next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first witness that the Prosecutor would call this morning is going to be presented via video link and we have requested a closed session in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand there are problems in establishing the video link. I wonder whether, to save time, we can call another witness, if your witnesses are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we would have to check on that. I understood that they were not going to arrive here until quarter to 9, with the Victim Witness Unit, so I am not sure if they are available at this point or not. Perhaps if we take a brief recess, we can check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. You have Mr. Fenwick who should be here close at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am not sure, your Honour. We can check and see. Mr. Fenwick's wife is extremely ill so he has been in and out and we had told him that he would be testifying tomorrow, so I am not sure if he is actually in the building or not. If the witnesses that are listed on the list as no. 2 and 3, if they are here and they are ready to proceed, it will just take us a moment to check. If your Honours want to wait, we can try to do that as everyone is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We can take a recess of, say, 10 minutes. We stand in recess until 9 o'clock. (8.48 am) (A short adjournment) (9.07 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would ask at this time that perhaps -- I cannot tell if the witness has actually placed his earphones on or not so that he is hearing the translations. Can the witness hear me at this point? Very well, at this time, perhaps if the witness can make the solemn declaration. (Closed session with video link) 25 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I understand you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask you to make the solemn declaration? IVICA DODLEK (affirmed)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: I am Ivica Dodlek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: 22nd March 1961.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your former profession?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: I used to be a professional policeman involved in criminology and now I am retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might tell us, when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: 1st January 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you retired, where were you stationed? Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: I had several jobs from the beginning of my career; I wonder what you are particularly interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we can just isolate it down to 1992, in the middle of 1992.

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: During 1992, I worked as a policeman at the police station in Vukovar. I was involved in crime and criminology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you enter the police force?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown MFI50, please. (Shown). Would you just look through MFI50, please, and can you tell me, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: It is an official document on an official -- of an official conversation that was held with Mr. Dragutin Berghofer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you go to the last page of the document and do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall taking this statement?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: Yes, but I do not remember everything about it. I do not remember all the details, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you take this statement?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: I took the statement at the Plitvice Motel in 1992 in the room of Mr. Dragutin Berghofer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you take it?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: It was not only me. It was my colleague who was working with me and myself and I did this because everything that we are familiar with had already taken place in Vukovar in 1991 and all of it was supposed to be collected and written down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was part of an ongoing investigation, was it?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: Well, not exactly an investigation, but there were some elements of an investigation involved, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you took this statement down, were you taking any notes contemporaneous with the discussion that you had with the witness?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: Yes, whatever the witness said -- rather not the witness, but Mr. Berghofer, whatever he said, I wrote down in my notebook and after that, I put it all into this official document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after did you do that?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: Well, you have to take into account the very difficult circumstances that we were working under, but a few days later, three or four days after that at the maximum, after the conversation took place, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you discuss the notes that you had taken with Mr. Berghofer at the time in order to see whether or not they were taken down accurately?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that quite well. After completing my conversation with him, I read the notes once again to see whether he disagreed with something so that I would not write the official document that would be different from what he had said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I do not want you to go into details of the statement, but were names given to you and places and events described, things that were familiar to you at the time when you took this statement down -- some of the things, I should say. Some of the names and events and places described, were they familiar to you when you took the statement down?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of taking this statement down according to the system under which you operated? Why did you take the statement down?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: The statement was taken down -- actually interviews were held with the witnesses who had the good fortune of surviving Ovcara and then after that, the courts would handle the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I tender the statement, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila. Cross-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I want to ask something, if I may. What did the witness show to Berghofer? His own notes or the official note when he was verifying it?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: My notes, the notes I jotted down when I was -- when I wrote this in my notebook. Then I read this out to him and then I copied it into the official documents so this is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so you showed it to him at that point in time, what you jotted down, and then after that you entered this in your official note?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Dokmanovic accused on the basis of that? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: Thank you.
utterances.text: I cannot tell really. I just know that it was processed, that we handed the official note in and I do not know whether anything was raised on that basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I am opposed to tendering this as evidence. For the same reasons I mentioned previously, according to our law, this is inadmissible. That is the reason. There are no other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to the law of Yugoslavia is not the test. In our submission, the law of Yugoslavia is not the test that applies in this Tribunal and we are not bound by it. It really boils down to a question of weight for your Honours, and certainly there can be arguments as to the weight of the document, but in our submission, a foundation is being laid for it and we submit that it is relevant and admissible in relation to this witness and in particular, Mr. Berghofer, who has already attested to the fact that he gave a statement and this witness has attested to the fact that he has taken it. In our submission, it does not matter that according to the law of Former Yugoslavia it may not have been admissible or it may be admissible. That does not determine the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you mention anything, beside the law of the Former Yugoslavia, this is effectively a previous consistent statement; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In common law jurisdictions, at least some common law jurisdictions, a previous consistent statement is not admissible as evidence of the facts in it. Why is it relevant here to know that the witness made an earlier complaint?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in our submission, the common law objection to previous consistent statements, in our submission, falls into a similar category to the objection based on the fact that it is not a document that would be admitted under the law of Yugoslavia, albeit for very different reasons. The law in the Former Yugoslavia, as I understand it and I do not profess to be an expert in that, but it goes to the fact that a second statement is obtained by the court itself, by an investigating judge, and the objection to this being tendered is because of that. It does not go to the issue, as I understand it, of prior consistent statements. In this jurisdiction, your Honours, it is admissible, we would submit, under the Rules. There is no provision in the Rules which of themselves say, prior consistent statements are not admissible. In many respects, the objection to the tendering of such matters at common law relates to issues connected with the jury. One is more concerned about statements or a number of statements being provided in this way, because one may be concerned about the reaction that the jury might have to it, and for those reasons, under the common law, the system of Rules relating to evidence has developed. We submit that is not appropriate here because your Honours are trained judges and you can receive a whole range of evidence which you can take into account and it really does boil down to, at the end of the day, how much weight you may attach to it. The primary concern in our submission that your Honours should have would go to its reliability, and it seems to us that if your Honours cannot be satisfied on reliability, that may be a factor which impacts upon its admissibility, because the court does not want to be in a situation where it has to make those sorts of judgements on a document which seems manifestly unreliable. Once that test is satisfied, which I submit it clearly has been in this case, then your Honours can consider it along with something else, along with any other piece of evidence that may come before you, and the restriction and very restrictive rules of evidence that apply in the common law system need not apply in this jurisdiction, because your Honours are no longer being concerned with a jury which is untrained in the law, being exposed to a range of evidence which they may not fully comprehend the significance of and may not be able to weigh and test in the same way that your Honours are trained to do. At the end of the day, as I say, your Honours may well take it upon yourselves to attribute to the document very little weight and say it is just not a matter which is going to be determinative on any issue, but your Honours should not approach it on the basis, in my respectful submission, of: let us exclude that; let us keep that out because there is some common law rule that might do that. In my submission, your Honours should let the document in and then deal with it, as I say, as a matter of weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is an objection here from the Defence and clearly you are right, when you say that the common law rules of evidence do not apply here, but clearly they are going to be of some use when you come to assess whether the document should be admitted. The issue in this case, as far as the particular witness is concerned, is identification, is it not? Therefore, the question is: is it going to assist us to know that a similar complaint was made in 1992? Is it relevant? Is it going to assist? I suppose there is a more general question as to whether these documents, these statements, prior consistent statements, should generally be admissible or not. If we admit this document in this case, is this going to be taken as a precedent for always admitting prior consistent statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As I understand, your Honour may have an objection based on prior consistent statement, but I do not understand that to be the objection of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That does not matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But I do not think I have to address the position in the Former Yugoslavia and it seems to me, your Honours, that we run into all sorts of difficulties if we find ourselves obliged to follow the laws of the Former Yugoslavia when it comes to the admissibility of evidence. It is a completely different regime and we have investigative prosecutors and judges working together in the formation of a dossier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? I follow that point entirely. Clearly the Rule is that here there is no other jurisdiction which governs the Rules of Evidence here. The Rules of Evidence here are the Rules of the Tribunal as it develops. The point that I was taking was the much narrower one based on the common law rule about prior consistent statements. It so happens that the rule in the Former Yugoslavia would apparently have the same effect, or might have the same effect. The danger might be if we admit this particular statement, and my mind is not made up at all, but I wish to address the point, is this going to lay a precedent for the admission of such statements normally --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that desirable?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission, it is entirely desirable, yes, because you are a totally different Tribunal to one where you are having lay persons determine the questions of fact based on the evidence that is put before them. There is much more sensitivity associated with filtering the evidence that goes before a jury because of the fact that they are not trained to deal with it, notwithstanding how detailed and careful a judge may be in directing the jury as to how they should treat the evidence. It is always open to the possibility that the jury may do with the evidence something that results in a miscarriage of justice. In my submission, your Honours should not approach the prosecutions in this case on that basis, relying on that criteria, because it is inappropriate. Your Honours, at the end of the day, need to carefully consider the totality of the evidence that is put before you and almost in a similar way to the admission of evidence de bene esse, your Honours should be not so restrictive in my respectful submission, in taking the evidence before you and then dealing with it on the totality. Otherwise we will be in a situation where the search for the truth, which is so fundamental to this jurisdiction, will be hampered by not being open to the ready acceptance of the evidence put forward by the parties. I do not think I can take it much further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Mumba would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just wanted to be clear in my mind, that the statement which this witness took was from Mr. Berghofer, the witness who had come?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness who had come to testify here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This statement according to this witness was taken in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: At the motel in the witness's room? In the witness's room? I mean -- no, in Mr. Berghofer's room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it was a hotel. I think the witness was a refugee at the time in a hotel in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because what bothers me is the fact that Mr. Berghofer was before the court and gave evidence in this very case and why the Rules here are not aligned to Yugoslavia or mainly the common law, I am worried about having a witness testify viva voce and then later on, having a statement which the same witness has taken earlier before the witness came before the court, because that puzzles me. I do not see why that should be the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can only say that it is -- as long as the issue of whether or not your Honours are satisfied that it is a credible and reliable piece of evidence, the fact that it is taken in 1992 and the fact that the witness has testified should not, in my respectful submission --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- be a basis for rejecting the evidence, but I think I have taken the matter about as far as I can and I accept that this is the first time certainly I have been involved in tendering it, so perhaps there is an issue involved in admitting it. But what I do say is that I do not think that your Honours need to be too concerned about the precedential effect of it, because I say that circumstances differ from case to case and what may appeal to the court as being admissible in one case may not in another, and I do not think that any decision made by your Honours on this would be binding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we make a ruling, I will turn first to Mr. Niemann and then ask a question of Mr. Fila. Mr. Niemann, of course this is based on the assumption, as was pointed out to my colleagues, my fellow judges, that of course we are not bound by any Rules of evidence of the Former Yugoslavia or common law countries or civil law countries. We have our own basic Rule 89 on the evidence and on the taking of evidence and on the probative value of evidence and of course this will govern our proceedings. However, Mr. Niemann, what is the relevance for the Prosecution of this particular statement? May I understand what is for you the relevance? Why do you regard this particular document relevant to your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it becomes more relevant, obviously, if we have an allegation of recent invention and then the Prosecution would be in a much stronger position in tendering a prior consistent statement in such circumstances. In our submission, it is very relevant that a witness said something to a police officer in a formal setting in 1992 and subsequently said it later on. It is relevant and it shows consistency. It shows that what the witnesses are saying is reliable. It means that your Honours can read this and compare it with what he said in the witness box and say, "There is a strain of consistency there which reinforces reliability." When your Honours look at it, you can say, "He said that then and he says it now, so that is reliable." My principal concern is just saying, "It is excluded by the common law, so therefore we ought to follow it automatically".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Fila, may I ask you to tell the court about the reasons why or the rationale behind the inadmissibility of the tendering of such documents under Yugoslav law so that we are clear about the position of your legal system?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am glad that we have a witness here who is a policeman so you can check on everything I say with him. This is an official note. I would kindly ask the interpreters to be as literal as possible. This is not a statement or a testimony. Mr. Niemann is talking about a statement that was taken from Mr. Berghofer. No statement was taken from him. If a statement had been taken from Mr. Berghofer, that statement would have been signed by him under our law in the common law in any jurisdiction and it would have the same weight under our legal system in the Former Yugoslavia, which was based on German law. We are not as intelligent as to have our own independent creation. Law enforcement bodies do not conduct investigations. They do not take statements. They just conduct interviews. This is called a preliminary interview with the witness. On the basis of what is written here, the investigating magistrate summons people and examines them and only then can they give a statement that Judge May is referring to. The police cannot take such formal statements. They just conduct interviews on the street, on a roof, on a tank, on a lorry -- wherever. So the precedent you are about to create is very dangerous. That is why I am vigorously opposing this, although the contents of this document are more to my advantage than to Mr. Niemann's. I will show you, whenever you ask me to, all the statements that prosecution witnesses, when they were interviewed in Sretiska Mitrovica, gave to the police and those statements were signed by them. This does not have any value under our system. If you do this now, I will then tender those statements as evidence and it is obvious that such statements were taken under duress, so that is why this is a potentially very dangerous precedent and that is what I wanted to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. (Judges confer).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Pursuant to Rule 89(d), a chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. The trial chamber rules that the tendering of this document in evidence is inadmissible. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions of the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand there is no objection to the witness being released. Thank you for coming. You may be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I suggest that we now take a recess. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will just say that I will not now call my next witness, which would have been doing the same thing, but I would like to indicate that to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us have a 20-minute recess and then we will reconvene. (10.22 am) (A short adjournment) (10.45 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann? Mr. Williamson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we would call Marin Vidic and we have requested this witness testify in closed session, but he will be using his real name and no other protective measures will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, while we are waiting for the witness, may I ask you whether you intend to call two witnesses tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And one on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That is all?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Well yes, sir. This will be our last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So no more witnesses today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: It is likely that this witness will go to the end of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether you can make an effort to come to a decision on the submissions by the Defence counsel, the five points I mentioned this morning, to decide whether or not you are ready to admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We will speak with the Defence as soon as court concludes today and try to resolve the outstanding issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, because we hope to do some planning this week for the future steps to be taken to see when the Defence counsel can start calling his witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As soon as the Prosecution has concluded their case, I have prepared my opening statement, but it is still in Serbian because I could not finish it because I did not know what would happen these days, so when the Prosecution concludes its case, you will receive my opening statement. You will also receive the order of my witnesses and my expert witnesses for the month of April. Within five days after the conclusion of their case. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Vidic. May I ask you to make the solemn declaration? MR. MARIN VIDIC (affirmed) Examined by MR. WILLIAMSON (In closed session)
